extracted.intended_audience: academics, scholarly-communications professionals, research evaluators, librarians, and university administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and reflections on rethinking metrics for evaluating scholarship (especially in the humanities and social sciences), proposing values-based indicators, workshop-driven development, and alternative evaluation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity (one of the Humanities Values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity is listed as a core humanities value and is specified with examples such as inclusivity, public good, social justice, equitable access, accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the HumetricsHSS "Humanities Values" graphic: equity includes inclusivity, public good, social justice, equitable access, accessibility. These are intended as foundations on which to build measures appropriate to humanities and social sciences evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness (one of the Humanities Values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Openness is named as a core value in the HumetricsHSS suite of values to inform humane indicators of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openness is a stated guiding value for designing metrics (no further elaboration on the page), implying measures should favor transparent, accessible scholarship and evaluation practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collegiality (one of the Humanities Values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collegiality is included as a core value intended to shape what is measured and rewarded in scholarship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a value, collegiality suggests metrics and incentives should recognize collaborative, community-minded behaviors and service to scholarly communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality (one of the Humanities Values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality is presented as a primary value to undergird humane metrics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality here functions as a substantive criterion distinct from simple citation counts — suggesting measures should capture intellectual rigor and contribution rather than raw numeric impact alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community (one of the Humanities Values)
rubrics_metrics.description: Community is listed among the five core values to inform metric design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community emphasizes measures that recognize public engagement, civic contribution, and the scholar's role within broader communities, not only academic citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metrics must be rooted in values that enrich scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: "If the metrics we use are to be capable of empowering innovative research along diverse pathways of intellectual development, they must be rooted in values that enrich the scholarly endeavor and practices that enhance the work produced."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric design should start from explicit scholarly values (equity, openness, collegiality, quality, community) so indicators empower diverse intellectual pathways rather than distort them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select measures to inspire desired behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: "We wanted to think about not just what we wanted to measure, but what we wanted to inspire." Metrics should be chosen with the behaviors they will incentivize in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design metrics to reward and encourage positive scholarly behaviors (e.g., mentoring, review, public engagement) rather than inadvertently incentivizing gaming or narrow publication strategies. Consider the question: what do we want to inspire?

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid perverse incentives; be responsible in design and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece stresses that metrics can drive negative behaviors and are biased from design to interpretation; therefore every use of metrics should be responsible to that design and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must account for known biases, field differences, and potential perverse incentives when creating or applying indicators, and must interpret numbers contextually rather than as unambiguous truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden what is rewarded — include reviewing, mentoring, and other contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: HumetricsHSS aims to expand the types of scholarly contributions that are rewarded in the academy (reviewing and mentoring, for example) so evaluation captures a wider range of labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation systems should incorporate measures (or narratives) that credit scholarly labor beyond publications and citations, e.g., peer review work, mentoring, service, public scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a flexible, iterative framework usable at multiple levels
rubrics_metrics.description: HumetricsHSS envisions "a flexible framework that institutions, departments and individuals could use"; the pilot is described as "exploratory not programmatic" and workshops are iterative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metric initiatives should be adaptable to local contexts, developed iteratively with stakeholder input, and offer tools usable by individuals, departments, and institutions rather than rigid, one-size-fits-all mandates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value the deliberative process of debating values even without consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if unanimity or consensus about core values is unlikely, the process of debating the values inherent in scholarship is valuable in itself for broader scholarly communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create time and space for structured reflection and discussion about evaluation values; the deliberative process can lead to better practices and increased awareness even absent uniform metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use subtler, discipline-appropriate indicators (e.g., altmetrics vs JIF)
rubrics_metrics.description: One proposed answer is to use more subtle measures of different kinds of outputs (more like Altmetrics than the JIF); applicability differs between humanities and STEM fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose indicators appropriate to disciplinary modes of dissemination and impact; prefer a mix of qualitative and quantitative signals tailored to field practices rather than relying on single blunt metrics like JIF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture a 'textured story' — narrative/contextual evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: HumetricsHSS aspires to present "a more textured story" about a scholar’s work, appreciating a rich diversity of scholarly contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate narrative elements (e.g., contextual explanations, portfolios, narrative CVs) alongside metrics to provide a fuller picture of scholarly contributions and trajectories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess intellectual milestones and mastery of dissemination, not only institutional milestones
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal anecdote suggests some scholars would prefer assessment based on intellectual milestones such as acquisition of knowledge and mastery of methods of dissemination rather than standard institutional tenure/promotion processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design evaluations that recognize individual intellectual development, mastery of communication/dissemination methods, and skill acquisition over purely time-based or institution-defined milestones.
